extracted.intended_audience: aspiring television writers / comedians who want to pitch, sell, and produce a TV pilot
extracted.subtask_short: selling and producing a TV pilot
extracted.subtask_description: A practical, experience-based walkthrough of the steps and decision points from pitching a show to having a pilot shot and considered for series pickup, with emphasis on development, casting, production, and notes/rewrites. Geared toward writers (especially comedy writers) navigating the studio/network system.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selecting studio/network partner
rubrics_metrics.description: Weigh offers and choose which studio/network to go with according to three criteria: 'Who really gets your show and will let you do it without fucking it up. Who is actually most likely to pick up the show. Who is paying you the most money (the worst reason to go with anyone).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize creative fit and likelihood of pickup over money; an executive or company that understands and will protect your show is preferable to the highest bidder. If no offers arrive, you remain unsold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outline requirements (before script)
rubrics_metrics.description: Write an outline: 'just a blow by blow description of each scene in paragraph form, which should include all plot points and any funny details or jokes you already have.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pass the outline to the studio/network and expect notes; a strong, well-tackled outline makes the later script stage easier and can reduce back-and-forth rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative notes-and-rewrite process
rubrics_metrics.description: After passing outline or script, you will get notes from studio then network; 'You take their notes and re-write it and if they are satisfied, you pass it in' and repeat until both are happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect multiple rounds. This is standard; sometimes it takes longer than outline stage. Stay responsive to notes but be aware over-rewriting can harm the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'rewriting to death' — maintain momentum
rubrics_metrics.description: A common failure point: 'The writer, studio and network bat the script around and it gets re-written to death, while other pilots are clicking along and improving.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the script is rewritten endlessly, executives lose interest and the project can stall or die. Preserve 'hotness' by resolving core story issues early (in outline) and avoiding endless incremental rewrites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script needs to 'stay hot' and appeal to executives
rubrics_metrics.description: If your script 'stays hot and people like it and you, it'll be declared finished and passed in to the network for consideration for pick up.' Top executives then read and may give 'big notes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive executive interest is crucial; notes from top-level executives can be a sign they think it's worth additional effort. Be prepared to defend and rework the project if given big notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showrunner requirement / staffing for showrunning
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are a 'strong enough and experienced enough writer, you are the show runner. But if you wrote the pilot but are a novice, you are also going to have to find a show-runner.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Realistically assess your ability to run a series while also performing (if applicable); hire or partner with an experienced showrunner if you cannot commit full-time to showrunning duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting director and casting process
rubrics_metrics.description: Hire a casting director (few good ones exist). Casting involves meeting many actors and presenting three top picks for every part. 'You make usually three top picks for every part... The three actors (per part) go to the network and audition... He/she/they pick one person and you are cast.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casting is time-consuming and competitive. Prepare three strong options per role because networks/studios will want choices; be ready for last-minute changes and actor passings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting priorities: funniness/acting vs big names
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives sometimes push big-name actors because they 'will help your show get on the air.' But some networks (HBO example) prioritize 'funninness and acting' over star power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance commercial considerations (names that sell) with creative fit; know your network's priorities and advocate for actors who best serve the material if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate test deals for actors
rubrics_metrics.description: Actors are often signed to a 'test deal' before the network sees them; you must negotiate deals with three actors per part even though only one will be hired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for the administrative and contractual complexity of holding multiple contingent deals; this is standard industry practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find a director — limited supply
rubrics_metrics.description: There are only a few good directors and many want them; hiring a skilled director is difficult but important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secure a director early if possible; a strong director helps stabilize the shoot and the translation of script to screen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Table read and early rehearsal feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Monday table read: network and studio watch actors read the script and give notes; notes can be devastating ('We don't know if the main point of the story is really that good or funny.'). Cast may be fired after this.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use table reads to identify major story or tone problems; be prepared to do immediate rewrites. Severe negative notes at table read often signal the pilot is in jeopardy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Runthroughs and incremental notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Tuesday/Wednesday runthroughs let the studio and network see the show 'on its feet' and they give more notes leading to additional rewrites and rehearsals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect iterative fixes during runthroughs; coordinate closely with the director and actors to implement changes quickly and keep the script stabilizing toward production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Script stabilization before blocking/camera rehearsals
rubrics_metrics.description: By the time 'the cameras are brought in and you block the show' the actors should be ready and 'the script should be stabilized. If you are still rewriting and casting at this point... you're pretty fucked.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to resolve casting and script issues well before camera blocking; late changes severely jeopardize production quality and schedule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot shoot dynamics and controlling notes during takes
rubrics_metrics.description: On shoot day (with audience): network and studio may give notes after every single take, causing multiple repeats and long shoots; audiences may leave if sessions run too long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan for tight rehearsals and try to limit on-set note-driven retakes; maintain good actor morale and audience experience to keep the shoot efficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing workflow and studio/network notes
rubrics_metrics.description: Editing process: 'The director edits first, then the showrunners. You pass in your edit to the studio, get notes and then the network.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect multiple edit passes and be prepared to re-edit in response to studio/network feedback. Have clear editorial leadership to synthesize notes and protect core story/ tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test screening and market research (network-dependent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some networks test pilots with audiences and provide elaborate data requiring re-edits; 'CBS... we had to wait while they tested the show' whereas 'HBO doesn't test their shows.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Know your network's approach to testing; if testing applies, be prepared to re-cut to address audience data and marketing experiments. Non-testing networks may require different defense strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defending the pilot to top executives
rubrics_metrics.description: After the finished pilot is passed in, top executives ('Carolyn Strauss and Chris Albrecht' example) may ask you to 'defend our thesis' and explain 'what we learned from doing the pilot and how we intended to execute a series.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be ready for meetings with top execs: articulate lessons from the pilot and a clear plan for executing the series. This can materially affect pickup decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major failure points to monitor (cast, showrunner, losing executive interest)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pilots can fail if you never find a good cast or showrunner, or if the project is rewritten to death and executives stop returning calls: 'Some pilots spin out and crash because a good cast or showrunner was never found.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize solving these structural problems early (secure showrunner, solid casting choices, protect executive interest) to reduce risk of project collapse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing, patience, and calendar realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Development and pickup decisions are seasonal and slow; 'This point is usually reached... right before the holidays' and network executives 'take a bunch of pilots home to read over the holidays.' Waiting is torturous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipate long waits, calendar-driven delays (e.g., Halloween to New Year), and the emotional toll of uncertainty; plan career and finances accordingly.
